what_its_for: Enasidenib is used to treat a type of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in adults whose cancer has come back or has not responded to other treatments. It works specifically in patients whose cancer cells have a change (mutation) in a gene called IDH2. Your doctor will test for this mutation before starting treatment.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with or without food. Try to take it at the same time every day. Do not crush, split, or chew the tablet. If you vomit after taking a dose, do not take another dose that day — just take your next scheduled dose as usual.
dosing: The usual dose is 100 mg taken by mouth once a day. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how well the medication is working and any side effects you experience. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your regular dose at the normal time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store enasidenib tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medication down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a medication take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medication, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use contraception during treatment and for 1 month after the last dose. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 1 month after the last dose. Tell your doctor about all other medications, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, as some drugs can interact with enasidenib.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: fever, chills, or signs of infection; sudden difficulty breathing or shortness of breath; rapid weight gain or swelling; bone or joint pain; confusion or changes in thinking; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); unusual tiredness or weakness; nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is severe or does not go away; or any new or unusual symptoms. These could be signs of a serious condition called differentiation syndrome, which can be life-threatening if not treated quickly.
when_it_works: Enasidenib may take several weeks to months before you start feeling better or before your doctor can tell if the medication is working. Blood tests will be done regularly to check how well the treatment is working. Do not stop taking the medication unless your doctor tells you to, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medication can harm an unborn baby and should not be used during pregnancy. Do not breastfeed while taking this medication. Liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver disease, as dose adjustments may be needed and your liver function will be monitored closely. Kidney problems: Let your doctor know if you have kidney disease. Older adults: Enasidenib has been used safely in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you closely for side effects. Children: This medication is not approved for use in children.
